A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Captain Safari method and OpenSafari study. The corresponding methods, equations, experiments, and figures can be matched reliably. V1 ends with references; v2 adds Supplementary Sections 7–10. The material included in both PDFs is readable.

before.justification: V1 reports original generation benchmarks, memory ablations, qualitative reconstructions, and a 50-participant human study in Sections 5.1–5.6 and Tables 1–2.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and adds the nearest-pose retrieval experiment in Supplementary Section 7 and Table 3.

M1.justification: The memory construction, pose-conditioned retrieval, DiT conditioning, two-stage training, and Equations 1–11 remain substantively unchanged. Specifying 3D RoPE and explicitly identifying ground-truth-derived inference memory provide additional documentation, without establishing a changed procedure. Nearest-pose retrieval is an added ablation, not a replacement for the proposed method.

E1.justification: The documented OpenSafari training and benchmark coverage remains unchanged. V2 Section 9 newly discusses moving-vehicle and ocean-wave demonstrations, but their videos are only linked externally. The PDFs do not establish whether these introduce distinct test scenarios beyond v1's existing vehicle and coastal examples.

E2.justification: V2 Table 3 adds an evaluated nearest-pose memory comparator alongside Captain Safari and its memory-free variant. Geometry Forcing, Real-CamI2V, and Wan2.2-5B-Control-Camera remain the main benchmark comparators. Newly cited world models are not added to the empirical comparison.

E3.justification: The documented benchmark retains 11,481 training clips, 787 test clips, five-second generation at 24 fps, the same training epochs, metrics, and human-study design. The SfM implementation, relative-pose canonicalization, and ground-truth memory source are newly disclosed settings, without an established revision to the existing protocol. The nearest-pose comparison introduces no separately documented evaluation protocol.

E4.justification: V1 tests memory versus no memory. V2 Supplementary Section 7 additionally tests whether selecting one nearest-pose memory feature can replace learned cross-attention retrieval. Table 3 directly supports the retrieval design by showing that this alternative performs worse than both existing variants.

E5.justification: V2 Section 5.4 introduces a Levene variance test, reporting p = 0.0439 alongside a 10% relative variance decrease for MEt3R. V1 reports no corresponding statistical test. This concerns variance, not significance of the mean improvement; neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds.

E6.justification: All numerical entries in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged. V2 Table 3 adds nearest-pose results, including FVD 1042.56, MEt3R 0.3810, and AUC@30 0.185, with worse performance across all six reported metrics than either retained variant. Section 5.4 also newly reports the 10% variance decrease and Levene p-value.

T1.justification: V2 Section 8 and Table 4 add an asymptotic complexity analysis: one-time retrieval costs O(|Mlocal|), while denoising adds O(ST|wt|) to the DiT cost with fixed-size world tokens. This is compared with full-memory cross-attention and concatenation. The original mathematical formulation remains unchanged, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and principal conclusion retain the same claims about pose-conditioned memory, OpenSafari, geometric consistency, trajectory following, and human preference. The expanded title emphasizes an existing component. Revised future-work statements and computational interpretations do not replace these central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 explains terminal-pose querying, interprets memory as a geometry prior trading perceptual scores for consistency, and attributes nearest-pose failures to viewpoint misalignment. It also discusses dynamic content through diffusion priors. The conclusion removes the explicit nontrivial-overhead caveat and identifies autoregressive memory built from generated frames as future work.

D1.justification: V2 newly specifies 3D RoPE, COLMAP's incremental mapper with a Simple Radial camera model, ground-truth-derived inference memory, and evaluation using the same SfM stack with first-frame canonicalization. Section 10 adds a repository pointer and explains that OpenSafari provides a curation pipeline rather than redistributed raw videos, for non-commercial academic use. These are documentation and access disclosures, not demonstrated changes to the experiments.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to RELIC, WorldPlay, Video World Models with Long-Term Spatial Memory, and RoFormer. Section 2.1 shifts its contrast with prior work toward compact, decoupled retrieval versus clip-bound memories or heavy point clouds. The earlier cited works remain represented, and the broader positioning is retained.

P1.justification: V2 expands the title, removes the work-in-progress notice, adds acknowledgements and Supplementary Sections 7–10, and makes localized explanatory and terminology edits. Most main-text paragraphs and the overall section sequence remain intact; this is not an extensive rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds Tables 3–4 for retrieval ablation and complexity, compacts the existing benchmark tables, and makes local layout adjustments. Figures 1–5 retain their visual content; Figure 4's caption gains a supplementary cross-reference. The visual organization remains largely unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 improves transparency through the ground-truth-memory disclosure, evaluation details, and dataset-access explanation. Table 3 supplies a useful control beyond v1's memory/no-memory comparison. The gains are limited: headline results and broad world-engine claims remain unchanged, generated-frame memory is deferred to future work, and the new constant-overhead language requires Section 8's qualification that retrieval itself still scales with memory length.
